**Cause:** the nightly path's only network call before that error is

```
curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/entireio/cli/releases?per_page=20   2>/dev/null
```

(`get_latest_nightly_version`, `scripts/install.sh:115-125`). stderr is discarded and `-f` prints nothing on an HTTP error, so any failure collapses into the misleading "check your internet connection". In the cloud sandbox the likely reason is **api.github.com's unauthenticated rate limit (60 req/hr per IP)** on a shared NAT egress — that also explains the intermittency ("often", not always). Second candidate: `api.github.com` not reachable through the sandbox proxy. Both are indistinguishable from the message today. `github.com` itself is clearly fine, since the asset download works from there when the version resolves.

**Workaround now** — paste this setup script; it resolves the tag from the releases Atom feed on `github.com` instead of the API, then hands the pinned version to the installer's download path:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
V=$(curl -fsSL https://github.com/entireio/cli/releases.atom \
    | grep -o 'releases/tag/v[^"]*nightly[^"]*' | head -1 | sed 's|releases/tag/v||')
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && cd "$(mktemp -d)"
curl -fsSL -O "https://github.com/entireio/cli/releases/download/v${V}/entire_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
curl -fsSL -O "https://github.com/entireio/cli/releases/download/v${V}/checksums.txt"
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing checksums.txt
tar -xzf entire_linux_amd64.tar.gz
install -m755 entire git-remote-entire ~/.local/bin/
```

Verified locally: the feed resolves `0.10.3-nightly.202608270913.f6091af37` and that asset URL is live.

**Proper fix** (want me to do it?): in `install.sh`, add a `releases.atom` fallback for both channels when the API call fails, surface curl's actual exit code/HTTP status instead of "check your internet connection", and add a `--version` flag so a pinned install needs no discovery at all. Also worth fixing regardless: `?per_page=20` silently yields no nightly if the 20 most recent releases happen to contain none.
But it also often failed for the normal installation `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`

You can configure an environment to allow or deny network access, set environment variables for the session, and run a setup script before Claude starts working.

Default environment carries Trusted network access: sessions reach package registries and other allowlisted domains, and nothing else through the session's network.

A setup script is an optional Bash script that runs before Claude Code launches, then gets cached so it doesn't re-run on subsequent sessions.

## Setup scripts

A setup script is a Bash script that runs when a new cloud session starts, before Claude Code launches. Use setup scripts to install dependencies, configure tools, or fetch anything the session needs that isn't pre-installed.

Scripts run as root on Ubuntu 24.04, so `apt install` and most language package managers work.

To add a setup script, open the environment settings dialog and enter your script in the **Setup script** field.

This example installs [ShellCheck](https://www.shellcheck.net/), which isn't pre-installed.

```bash theme={null}
#!/bin/bash
apt update && apt install -y shellcheck
```

### Script requirements

A setup script has three constraints to write around:

* **Exit zero**: if the script exits non-zero, the session fails to start. Append `|| true` to non-critical commands so an intermittent install failure doesn't block the session.
* **Finish within five minutes**: keep the script's total runtime under roughly five minutes so the [environment cache](#environment-caching) can build. Run independent installs in parallel with `&` and `wait`, and move any single download that won't fit into a [SessionStart hook](#setup-scripts-vs-sessionstart-hooks) that launches it in the background.
* **Network access for installs**: package installs need to reach registries. The default **Trusted** level covers [common package registries](#default-allowed-domains) including npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and crates.io; with **None** network access, installs fail.

### Environment caching

The setup script runs the first time you start a session in an environment. After it completes, Anthropic snapshots the filesystem and reuses that snapshot as the starting point for later sessions. New sessions start with your dependencies, tools, and Docker images already on disk, and skip the setup script step. This keeps startup fast even when the script installs large toolchains or pulls container images.

=== security proxy ===
### Security proxy

Cloud sessions in Anthropic-hosted environments run behind an HTTP/HTTPS network proxy for security and abuse prevention purposes; in a [self-hosted environment](/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-deploy#default-deny-egress), outbound traffic leaves through your own network boundary instead. All outbound internet traffic from an Anthropic-hosted session passes through this proxy, which provides:

* Protection against malicious requests
* Rate limiting and abuse prevention
* Content filtering for enhanced security
* A DNS-level audit trail of requested hostnames

## What's available in cloud sessions

In Anthropic-hosted environments, each session gets a fresh virtual machine (VM) running Ubuntu 24.04 on x86\_64, regardless of your own operating system and CPU architecture, with your repository cloned and common toolchains pre-installed. When a dependency provides precompiled binaries, such as Ruby gems with native extensions or prebuilt Python wheels, use its x86\_64 Linux build to match the VM. This section covers the Anthropic-hosted defaults, the built-in GitHub tools, how to [run tests and services](#run-tests-start-services-and-add-packages), and the [resource limits](#resource-limits) each VM gets.

Several of my assumptions were wrong. The docs describe a specific mechanism that makes this deterministic, not flaky-network.

**What actually happens.** All GitHub traffic in Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions goes through a dedicated **GitHub proxy**, *independent of the environment's network access level*, and: "GitHub API and release-asset requests reach only repositories attached to the session, so **a setup script that downloads release assets from an unattached repository gets a 403**." `install.sh` calls `api.github.com/repos/entireio/cli/releases…`, gets 403, `-f` yields empty output, stderr is `2>/dev/null`'d, and you get "check your internet connection."

**What I got wrong:**

1. **"Full network access should allow it."** No — GitHub traffic bypasses the access-level allowlist entirely. Setting Full changed nothing, which is why it fails at a level that lists `api.github.com` as allowed anyway.
2. **Rate limiting on a shared egress IP.** Not needed as an explanation, and probably not it — the documented failure is a repo-scope 403.
3. **Both workarounds I gave you are likely broken too.** I claimed "github.com works since asset downloads succeed" — I had no evidence for that; your run never reached the download step. `releases.atom` and `releases/download/...` go through the same GitHub proxy and the same repo-scope check. Don't use those snippets.
4. **My DNS/IPv6 check was beside the point.** I was looking for a routing difference between `api.github.com` and `github.com`; interception is by hostname at a proxy, so their sharing 140.82.121.x proves nothing.
5. **Suggesting `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the env-var field.** Worse than useless here: when the proxy handles auth, `GITHUB_TOKEN` reads as the literal placeholder `proxy-injected`, and `fetch_github_json` (`install.sh:92-99`) tests only for non-emptiness — so it would send `Authorization: Bearer proxy-injected`. Separately, user-set env vars are reported empty inside setup scripts ([#63541](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/63541)).

What survives: the failing call is that one `curl`, and the error text is misleading because stderr is discarded.

**Falsifiable prediction, worth one check:** it should *succeed* in a session attached to `entireio/cli` and fail in sessions attached to any other repo. If it also fails on `entireio/cli` sessions, the repo-scope explanation is wrong and something else is going on.

**Workaround that avoids GitHub entirely** — `proxy.golang.org` is on the Trusted allowlist and is not the GitHub proxy:

```bash
V=$(curl -fsS https://proxy.golang.org/github.com/entireio/cli/@v/list \
      | grep nightly | sort -t. -k4 | tail -1)          # or: @latest for stable
GOBIN=$HOME/.local/bin go install "github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@${V}" || true
GOBIN=$HOME/.local/bin go install "github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@${V}" || true
```

Tested locally against `v0.10.3-nightly.202608270913.f6091af37`: builds and reports `Entire CLI 0.10.3-nightly.202608270913.f6091af37`, so version stamping survives `go install`. Caveats: watch the 5-minute setup-script budget (cold build, plus a toolchain download if the image's Go is below go.mod's 1.26.6), and the `|| true` keeps a failure from blocking session start.

**Real fix for the product:** serve the version manifest and the binaries from `entire.io` instead of GitHub releases. That path goes through the ordinary security proxy, so it works at Full for any session regardless of attached repo. A GitHub-side fallback inside `install.sh` can't fix this, since the whole host family is scoped the same way. Independent of that, `install.sh` should stop discarding curl's stderr, report the HTTP status, and not send a `proxy-injected` placeholder as a Bearer token.

## What the diff does

**1. `http_get` replaces `fetch_github_json` — the key change is dropping `-f`.**

`curl -fsSL` makes curl exit silently on any HTTP error, so the body — the part where GitHub says *why* — is thrown away. Now it's `-sSL -w '\n%{http_code}'`: fetch unconditionally, append the status code as a final line, split it off, and if it isn't 2xx print `HTTP <status> from <url>` plus GitHub's own `"message"` field. That single change is what turns "check your internet connection" into "API rate limit exceeded for 35.239.245.65."

**2. `http_effective_url` — a redirect probe.** `-o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}'` follows redirects and prints where it landed, no body needed.

**3. Two `*_from_web` resolvers, now the primary path.**

- `resolve_stable_from_web`: `github.com/entireio/cli/releases/latest` 302s to `/releases/tag/v0.10.2`, so the redirect target *is* the version. The `case` guard returns failure rather than a garbage version if the URL doesn't look like a tag page.
- `resolve_nightly_from_web`: `releases.atom` lists releases newest-first; grep the first `-nightly.` tag link.

Neither host is `api.github.com`, so neither is rate limited.

**4. `resolve_from_api` — the old logic, demoted to fallback.** Same endpoints, still honors `GITHUB_TOKEN` (with `${curl_opts[@]+…}` so an empty array doesn't trip `set -u` on macOS bash 3.2). **5. `get_latest_version` — one entry point, ordered web → API → fail loudly.** The final error tells you to look up at what GitHub actually said and points at the releases page for a manual install. `main` loses its channel `if/else` and calls this instead.
